title: Distinct OR Values Over All Slices
statement:
You get an array of non-negative integers nums. For every non-empty contiguous slice, take the bitwise OR of all its elements.

Return how many different values these ORs produce.

examples.why: Single slices give 1, 2, 4. Pairs give 3 and 6. The whole array gives 7. All six differ.
There are six slices, but their ORs are only 1, 2 and 3. Count values, not slices.

hints: Fix where a slice ends. How many different ORs can slices ending at i have?
Extending a slice to the left can only turn bits on, never off. Each new distinct value has at least one more bit set.
So the set of ORs of slices ending at i has at most about 30 values. Build it from the set for i − 1 by OR-ing each value with nums[i], plus nums[i] alone.

explain.intuition:
Group the slices by their last index i. Start at i and extend to the left: the OR can only gain bits. Whenever the value changes it gains at least one bit, and there are only about 30 bits, so the slices ending at i produce at most ~31 different ORs.

That set is easy to update. Every slice ending at i is either [nums[i]] alone or a slice ending at i − 1 extended by one element. So cur(i) = { nums[i] } ∪ { v | nums[i] : v in cur(i − 1) }. Add every value of every cur to one global set and return its size.
steps: Keep cur, the set of ORs of slices ending at the previous index, and all, every OR seen.
For each x: build next = { x } plus v | x for every v in cur.
Add everything in next to all, then set cur = next.
pitfalls: Counting slices instead of distinct values.
Rebuilding each slice's OR from scratch in a triple loop. Even the O(n²) version times out at 50 000.
Forgetting the slice made of x alone when building next.

solutions.title: Every start, extend to the right
solutions.idea: For each start, extend the slice one element at a time and add the running OR to a set.

solutions.title: Small set of ORs ending here
solutions.idea: The ORs of slices ending at i form a set of at most ~31 values. Build it from the previous set, and collect all values globally.

followups: Does the same trick work for AND? What about XOR, and why not?
Return the number of slices whose OR equals a given value k.
